title: 🌿 Orundel — Second Age Rivers, Forests, Courts & Conflict
rawNotionMarkup: Orundel • complete Second Age in Avarran retrospective Years 1–1,437. The names and boundaries of Orundel's own historical eras remain undecided. This chronicle places distinct river, tropical woodland, highland, steppe and maritime societies in shared time without pretending they were one kingdom. It predates, and does not duplicate, the Reed-Crown League and War of Three Locks established for the final 116 years. ## A river that could no longer be read (Years 1–110) As the Great Cataclysm reshaped lunar power, communities around the river mosaics of Orundel struggled to anticipate floods. Some ancient magical signs were not merely weak but actively misleading; other local workings remained functional, and the World's Breath continued independently. The Lost-Stair Flood, remembered in a cluster of towns but not a global disaster, caught lowland residents where a protective water ward failed. A group of Tigerfolk medicine apprentices, Human boatbuilders and Goblin ferry families opened a disused warehouse as a clinic. The clinic's founder, Saluma Reed-Hands, was a Human boatwright who insisted that free beds be counted by available space rather than by a magistrate's caste register. A local governor later tried to charge the clinic for harbor frontage. Neighbors protected it by linking boats across its landing, creating the custom of the Chain of Safe Boats. In the upper forests, Mushroom folk investigated changes in rot, soil and water by direct study, not a collective hive mind; Gnomes worked alongside them on drainage. Their first Living Soil Notebooks recorded what they could actually observe. Some human settlers blamed fungus communities for ordinary blight and destroyed several gardens, even when the gardens had supplied food during shortages. An independent Shade Court, formed by a handful of resident households of different peoples, heard testimony and ordered reparations from some attackers; other communities never saw justice. ## Roads between unlike worlds (Years 111–321) ### The Reed-Gold Assembly A network of river towns developed the Reed-Gold Assembly, a rotating meeting of independent ports that agreed on physical flood marks, emergency boat access, river weights and seasonal taxes. It did not rule the whole continent; inland plateau cities, rainforest federations and Centaur steppe societies had their own rulers. Voting was unequal, favoring wealthy ports. the Silt-Marked Petition was prepared by a group of poorer boat crews, Harpy scouts, and Foxfolk legal clerks who demanded that disaster crews receive a legal voice. The Assembly adopted a limited right to testify without granting equal political votes. A Tigerfolk cartographer, Neris of Seven Bends, developed river charts combining current soundings, physical landmark sketches and recently observed lunar conditions. Her rival claimed she had stolen techniques from a less prestigious Merfolk navigator. Her surviving annotations credit several Merfolk and Goblin collaborators, making her celebrated work also evidence that famous single authors often depended on unrecognized people. ### The highland refuge quarrels In upland regions some Giant, Kobold and Human communities argued over access to stone shelters during changing weather. A mountain lord turned several refuges into toll houses; a Kobold family called the Red-Handle Builders enlarged ventilation shafts and enabled trapped families to escape when a ward misfired. An independent Minotaur mediator, Karrum Vale, negotiated a new contract that paid maintainers and required emergency shelter for travelers. That agreement lasted for two generations before a later ruler ignored it. Its failure did not erase the lives it had saved. ## Early Wonder: a thousand directions (Years 322–575) Different Orundel towns grew rich as newly mastered moon-fragment arts improved botanical knowledge, metalwork, civic architecture and navigation. The House of Patient Rivers was a riverside teaching college open to many occupations, though fee waivers depended on guild sponsorship. A group of students organized the Night Lessons, teaching calculation, law and medicine to workers after market hours. Several teachers were dismissed; some joined a newly chartered public school and helped create practical health instruction independent of patrons. In tropical forest regions, the Rain-Bark Confederacy, a loose alliance of villages and forest councils, limited clearing of certain watersheds after a series of damaging floods. Not all villages agreed: some wanted more farmland and suspected the restrictions protected powerful timber traders. Ent witnesses advised some council gatherings, but they did not rule the communities, and Aelwyn rites of reciprocity remained separate. A forest healer, Vasha Half-Sky, criticized both wealthy clearers and elites who forbade the poor to gather medicines. Her Gatherer's Measure granted seasonal access to specified plants without opening sacred groves to wholesale destruction. It was a negotiated compromise, not a universal law. ### The great demand for copper light A guild of Gnome, Goblin, Human and Tigerfolk artisans developed intricate safe-light systems, pairing new lunar enchantments with ordinary oil and repair access. Their lamps enriched port life, theater, schooling and night medicine; temple and noble interests sought monopoly licenses. the Copper-Light Walkout followed when miners and glassworkers objected to pay withheld for equipment alleged to be magically perfected. Workers' threatened strike led to a partial accident-compensation schedule. It left large inequalities intact, but made public the names of people previously listed merely as workshop property. ## Mid-Wonder: the price of straight roads (Years 576–910) ### The Green-Step Principalities Small, competing principalities on the forest-steppe transition financed causeways and enriched trade through dense river markets. Their rulers varied: elected councils, hereditary houses, military commanders who kept temporary rule for too long. These were not modern Orundel kingdoms renamed, and they did not form one universal empire. In the eastern steppe, Centaur associations negotiated rights of passage and irrigation with settled farming villages; some cases ended in open councils and others in punitive fighting. A prince in one Green-Step state began seizing land from mixed communities to build a grand enchanted highway, claiming new lunar engineering would make agriculture unnecessary along the route. Farmers, including Pigfolk, Cowfolk, Goblin and Human households, resisted through petitions. A few organized armed defense and were beaten; surviving witnesses called this episode the Four-Market Suppression. One governor later restored some fields when a neighboring city refused to buy grain seized under the decree. The reversal was incomplete, but it marked the beginning of the Bounded Works Statute, requiring public assessment of a major construction project's effects on local water and farms. Skilled engineers could support the statute without being enemies of magic. ### The Amber Ledger Trials In a southern river city, trade officials falsified measures for ore and medicine and blamed bad magic when shortages appeared. Magistrate Eren Kha, an independent Human judge, took testimony from a Merfolk pilot, a Foxfolk auditor, several wounded dockhands and a Mushroom folk apothecary. Their evidence exposed an organized fraud. Witnesses were threatened, and the first trial was annulled after political interference. A later public inquiry made independent scales and river sampling mandatory at some docks. Corruption survived elsewhere, and the affected families carried losses that no verdict fully repaid. ## Late Wonder: universities and broken charters (Years 911–1,321) The Six Rivers Symposium brought scholars and practical workers from different parts of Orundel together to compare rival medical and lunar-magical claims. It did not appoint a universal master of magic. Tigerfolk and Gnome researchers, Centaur astronomers, Lionfolk legal thinkers, Merfolk current observers and other people held incompatible theories. A prominent patron demanded that results be hidden from competing cities; a group of graduate teachers circulated a Public Ledger of Failed Cures anonymously, helping healers recognize unsafe practices. Court officials prosecuted some contributors; others preserved their findings in open clinics. In the highland margins, Kobold and Giant builders found work alongside other peoples and also faced exploitative contracts. Harpy cliff towns developed independent warning signals, theater and local political contests, not simply messenger jobs for city kings. Different Mushroom folk councils contested whether medicinal fungi should be freely shared or locally controlled. A village grew prosperous on new lunar farming techniques, while a neighboring family unable to afford training lost its land to creditors. Such contradictions were typical: the broadly prosperous millennium had space for terrible injustice. ### The weather-watchers' promise After a major storm damaged several unrelated ports, river scouts, Merfolk current keepers and Harpy watchers established the Promise of Open Warning: a local obligation to share imminent danger information even with rival towns. The policy saved many travelers and was sometimes broken for strategic advantage. Its imperfect legacy later influenced river warning practice without being declared the foundation of the Reed-Crown League of Years 1,322–1,437. ## The final Avarran date band (Years 1,322–1,437) The Reed-Crown League, its internal political differences, and War of Three Locks are recorded in the existing Era of Fire — Kingdoms, Peoples & Cultural Chronicle (Second Age, 1322–1437). They are independent of the Green-Step Principalities and the Four-Market Suppression unless later creator decisions establish a relationship. The world-shaking earthquakes of Second Age Year 1,437 ended the Age; no species went extinct. A full regional death toll, exact Orundel states destroyed, and the name locals gave this era remain open. There were no Orcs in Second Age Orundel.
